title: Venus: Facts

title: Mars: Facts
notes: Cited for: Mars looks red because of iron oxide (rust) in its soil and dust.

title: Planets
notes: Cited for: inner rocky planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars); gas giants Jupiter and Saturn; ice giants Uranus and Neptune.

title: Jupiter: Facts
notes: Cited for: Jupiter is the largest planet and more than twice as massive as all other planets combined.

title: Saturn: Facts
notes: Cited for: Saturn's rings are made mostly of chunks of ice with some rock.

title: What Causes the Seasons?
notes: Cited for: seasons are caused by Earth's ~23.5° axial tilt, not distance from the Sun; hemispheres have opposite seasons.

title: Earth: Facts
notes: Cited for: Earth is closest to the Sun (perihelion) in early January. Confirm exact page wording.

title: Moon: Facts
notes: Cited for: average Earth–Moon distance ~384,400 km; the Moon is tidally locked, always showing the same face.

title: Moon Phases
notes: Cited for: phases come from how much of the sunlit half we see; a full cycle takes about 29.5 days.

title: Eclipses
notes: Cited for: solar eclipse (Moon between Sun and Earth); lunar eclipse (Earth's shadow falls on the Moon); Sun ~400× wider and ~400× farther than the Moon.

title: What Is a Light-Year?
notes: Cited for: a light-year is a distance (~9.46 trillion km); Proxima Centauri is ~4.2 light-years away.

title: Stars
notes: Cited for: stars form in clouds of gas and dust; hotter stars are bluer; the Sun will become a red giant then a white dwarf; massive stars can end in supernovae.

title: Galaxies
notes: Cited for: Milky Way ~100,000 light-years across; Andromeda ~2.5 million light-years away; the observable universe holds billions of galaxies.

title: How Old Is the Universe?
notes: Cited for: the universe is about 13.8 billion years old.

title: How many oceans are there?
notes: Cited for: one global ocean; 71 percent of Earth covered by water; four historic oceans plus the Southern Ocean as the fifth.

title: How Much Water is There on Earth?
notes: Cited for: about 71 percent of Earth's surface is water-covered.

title: Continent
notes: Cited for: seven continents and their order by size; Asia holds almost a third of the land; Antarctica has no permanent population; Australia smallest and flattest.

title: There's a new ocean now: can you name all five?
notes: Cited for: National Geographic began recognizing the Southern Ocean, encircling Antarctica, as the fifth ocean on World Oceans Day (June 8) 2021.

title: What is the largest ocean on Earth?
notes: Cited for: Pacific is the largest and deepest basin; all continents could fit in it; ranking Atlantic, Indian, Southern, Arctic.

title: Pacific Ocean
notes: Cited for: the Pacific occupies about one-third of the globe's surface and exceeds the whole land surface.

title: Selecting a Map Projection
notes: Cited for: every flat map has distortion; Mercator 1569; Africa is fourteen times larger than Greenland; equal-area maps keep true relative sizes but distort shape.

title: Mercator projection
notes: Cited for: introduced by Gerardus Mercator in 1569; straight lines are lines of constant bearing for navigation; areas far from the Equator appear too large.

title: What is latitude?
notes: Cited for: latitude measures distance north or south of the Equator, 0 to 90 degrees; latitude lines are parallel; Equator divides the hemispheres.

title: What is longitude?
notes: Cited for: longitude measures distance east or west of the prime meridian through Greenwich; meridians run pole to pole and meet at the poles.

title: International Prime Meridian Conference
notes: Cited for: the 1884 Washington conference chose the Greenwich meridian as 0 degrees longitude; countries had used their own prime meridians; standard time zones adopted.

title: What is at Zero Degrees Latitude and Zero Degrees Longitude?
notes: Cited for: 0 degrees latitude, 0 degrees longitude is in the Atlantic Ocean in the Gulf of Guinea; Null Island nickname; faulty records assigned 0,0.

title: Equator
notes: Cited for: Equator at 0 degrees latitude, halfway between the poles; divides the hemispheres; Sun directly over it at the equinoxes.

title: Tropics
notes: Cited for: Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn at 23.5 degrees north and south of the Equator.

title: Tropic of Cancer
notes: Cited for: about 23 degrees 27 minutes N; the Sun is directly over it at the June solstice, its northernmost overhead position.

title: Tropic of Capricorn
notes: Cited for: about 23 degrees 27 minutes S; the Sun is directly over it around December 21, its southernmost overhead position.

title: Lahaina Noon
notes: Cited for: when the Sun is exactly overhead an upright object casts no shadow; the Sun is never directly overhead outside the tropics; Hawaii is the only US state where it happens.

title: Arctic Circle
notes: Cited for: about 66 degrees 30 minutes N; the Sun does not set about June 21 or rise about December 21; continuous day or night grows to six months at the pole; tilt of about 23.5 degrees.

title: Antarctic Circle
notes: Cited for: Antarctic Circle at 66 degrees 30 minutes S, with at least one day of continuous daylight and of darkness a year.

title: Standard Time
notes: Cited for: communities once kept separate local times; railways made standard time urgent; 24 zones on meridians 15 degrees apart from Greenwich; borders follow political boundaries.

title: International Date Line
notes: Cited for: date line follows the 180th meridian for most of its length; travelers going west set calendars a day ahead, east a day back.

title: Date Line
notes: Cited for: date line roughly follows the 180-degree meridian halfway around from the prime meridian; west is one day ahead; it curves around Kiribati.

title: The Sun, Earth and Cardinal Directions
notes: Cited for: the four cardinal directions; the Sun rises roughly in the east and sets roughly in the west; east and west at right angles to north and south.

title: Why does the Sun rise in the east?
notes: Cited for: Earth rotates toward the east, so the Sun rises in the east and moves westward across the sky.

title: Earth's Magnetic Field (compass needles)
notes: Cited for: Earth is like a giant magnet; compass needles follow magnetic field lines; Magnetic North Pole differs from the Geographic North Pole and moves; magnetic declination.

title: Compass (navigational instrument)
notes: Cited for: a magnetized needle aligns with Earth's magnetic field; needles point to a point near, not at, the North Pole; variation or declination varies from place to place.

title: Wandering of the Geomagnetic Poles
publisher: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information
notes: Cited for: the magnetic dip poles migrate over time.

title: Topographic Maps
notes: Cited for: contour lines connect points of the same elevation above a reference surface, usually mean sea level; spacing shows steepness.

title: Topographic Maps
notes: Cited for: contour lines are lines of equal elevation; the closer the contours, the steeper the slope.

title: Mount Everest
notes: Cited for: Everest is the highest mountain in the world at about 8,849 m; 2020 China and Nepal joint measurement.

title: Plateau
notes: Cited for: a plateau is a flat, elevated landform that rises sharply above the surrounding area on at least one side.

title: Valleys, Information and Facts
notes: Cited for: valleys are low areas carved by water and ice; rivers carve V shapes and glaciers grind them into U shapes.

title: Delta
notes: Cited for: a delta is a flat, low-lying plain at a river's mouth built from sediment dropped as the river slows; named for the Greek letter delta.

title: Space Segment
notes: Cited for: at least 24 operational GPS satellites; each circles Earth twice a day at about 20,200 km; users can view at least four satellites from virtually anywhere.

title: GPS: The Global Positioning System
notes: Cited for: satellites transmit one-way signals with position and time; receivers calculate three-dimensional position and time; civilian service freely available to all users.

title: Global Positioning System
notes: Cited for: each satellite transmits its position and time; a receiver finds its position from how long the signals took to reach it.

title: The Global Positioning System (Geodesy tutorial)
notes: Cited for: satellites carry very precise clocks; distance equals signal speed times travel time; four satellites needed, three for position and one for the receiver's clock error.

title: What Is An Antipode In Geography?
notes: Cited for: antipode definition; noon at one is midnight at the other; opposite hemispheres; about 15% of land is antipodal to land; Spain's antipodes in New Zealand.

title: Antipodes World Map & Why You Can't Dig To China From The US
notes: Cited for: digging through Earth from the US leads to the Indian Ocean, not China; about 15% of land is antipodal to land.
